newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks seen mixed to higher, IBM up.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks seen mixed to higher, IBM up.

text.p: Wall Street stocks are seen opening mixed to higher Thursday, with strength in shares of International Business Machines Corp giving a lift to the Dow industrials.

IBM was trading at 148 ahead of the opening bell, traders said, up from Wednesday's close of 142-3/8. Merrill Lynch raised its rating on the stock to near-term buy from neutral while keeping it a long-term buy, a Merrill source said.
"With prospects for a good economy continuing, IBM will perform well," one analyst said.
The analyst, Westfalia Investments director of research Peter Cardillo, said, "When all is said and done, IBM will help the tech group. Maybe the pressure on the techs will abate on IBM's outlook."
Cardillo said that weekly jobless claims, due out at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, would set the tone for the bond market and have an impact on stocks.

"Today and tomorrow, the stock market will closely follow bonds. Any failure of the long bond yield to move lower would probably indicate we have reached the upper end of this rally and could start to retreat to 6500," he said.
In Tokyo, the Nikkei Average was down 37.40 points, or 0.20 percent, at 18,698.07.
In London, the FTSE 100 Index was down 9.5 at 4378.2.

Among U.S. shares traded in London, IBM was up one at 143-3/8 while Halliburton Co added 1/8 to 74 after the company reported first quarter earnings per share of $0.65 versus a First Call mean estimate of $0.63 a share.
The dollar held on to small gains above 126 yen in Tokyo and edged off its highs in Europe.
U.S. Treasuries were mixed, with the long bond up 2/32 to yield 7.09 percent.

The Wall Street Journal's Heard on the Street writes that three years after his victory over Barry Diller for Paramount Communications, Viacom Inc VIA.A Chairman Sumner Redstone is struggling to persuade Wall Street that his stock is oversold.

The New York Times Market Place writes that the Toronto Stock Exchange yesterday closed its trading floor and switched entirely to computers, hoping to lower costs, protect its share of the market and at least partly overcome the embarassment it suffered last month when frenzied trading in a troubled stock repeatedly shut down the exchange.
